summary: For ages 7-8: find 10 more/less and 100 more/less than any number up to 1000, mentally, by reasoning about which digit changes. +10 steps the tens digit, +100 steps the hundreds digit, and the other digits stay the same \u2014 except at a boundary where a column 'fills up' and rolls over (e.g. 190 + 10 = 200, where the tens roll 9\u21920 and carry into the hundreds). Learners should name which digit changes and explain why, keeping the method place-value based rather than counting in ones.
misconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding 100 but stepping the tens).
Failing at boundaries — 190 + 10 giving '1100' or '190' unchanged instead of 200.
Counting on in ones instead of jumping the place.
Assuming only one digit ever changes, so mishandling the carry when a column rolls over.

activities.title: Digit stepper: watch one column respond
steps: Start with a three-digit number shown in an H|T|O place-value chart (e.g. 638).
Predict which digit will change before pressing +100, then press it and check: only the hundreds digit ticks up (638\u2192738) while tens and ones stay fixed.
Repeat with +10, -10, -100 on several numbers, each time saying aloud which column changes and which stay the same.
Contrast +10 and +100 side by side on the same starting number to track that they act on different columns.
activities.insight: Adding/subtracting 10 acts on the tens column and adding/subtracting 100 acts on the hundreds column; when no column rolls over (as with 638), the other digits hold still. This is a place-value jump, not counting on in ones. Boundary cases such as 190 + 10 come in the next activity.

activities.title: Boundary roll-overs: when a column fills up
steps: Start at 190 and find 10 more. Watch (or work out on a base-ten mat/number line) the tens roll 9\u21920 and a ten carry up to make one more hundred, so 190 becomes 200.
Find 10 less than 305: the tens are 0, so a hundred must be exchanged for ten tens before removing one \u2014 305, 295.
Find 10 more than 695: the tens fill up (9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens), which rolls over to make a new hundred, so the hundreds go 6\u21927 and the ones stay 5 \u2014 695 becomes 705.
Find 100 more than 950 and decide whether the answer is still a three-digit number (it becomes 1050, which rolls into a new thousands column).

For each, say which digits moved and why, e.g. for 190 + 10: 'the tens filled up, so they rolled to 0 and added one to the hundreds'; for 305 - 10: 'there were no tens, so I exchanged a hundred for ten tens and took one away'; for 950 + 100: 'the hundreds filled up, so they rolled to 0 and made one thousand.'
activities.insight: The rule 'only one digit changes' has a meaningful exception: when a column reaches its limit (a 9 going up, or a 0 going down), it rolls over and carries/borrows into the next column. These boundary cases are the interesting core of the skill, not exceptions to memorise.

activities.title: Fluency practice with boundary items
steps: Answer quick fill-in items: '100 more than 638 = __', '10 less than 305 = __', '100 more than 950 = __'.
Answer 'which digit changes?' when finding 100 more (or 10 less) for a given number.
Mix plain cases (456 + 100) with boundary cases (190 + 10, 695 + 10, 305 - 10) so the two are not predictable.
Optionally use a slider on a 0-1000 line to land on answers and self-check.
activities.insight: Once the place-value reasoning is understood, the skill can become quick mental recall, applied reliably even when a boundary forces a regroup.

checkQuestion: Ask quickly and watch the method: '100 more than 456? ... 10 less than 305? ... 10 more than 695? ... 100 more than 950?' The last three cross a boundary — watch what happens to the neighbouring digits.
checkAnswer: 556; 295; 705; 1,050 — changing only the right digit unless a boundary forces a regroup, and regrouping correctly across it.
